scenes.title: Morocco
scenes.subtitle: A history told only by its sources

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: In the 5th century BCE, the city-state of Carthage extended its hegemony over the coastal areas.

scenes.caption: Photo 1919 · Marrakech
scenes.text: Indigenous Berber monarchs ruled the territory from the 3rd century BCE until 40 CE, when it was annexed to the Roman Empire.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: In the mid-5th century CE, it was overrun by Vandals, before being recovered by the Byzantine Empire in the 6th century.

scenes.caption: Photo 1879
scenes.text: Mogador is known to have been a Phoenician colony by the early 6th century BCE.

scenes.caption: Photo 1879
scenes.text: Mauretania was an independent tribal Berber kingdom on the Mediterranean coast of north Africa, corresponding to northern modern-day Morocco from about the 3rd century BCE.

scenes.caption: Photo 1879
scenes.text: The earliest known king of Mauretania was Baga who lived around 225 BCE and possibly belonged to an older dynasty.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: After allying with the Sufri Kharijite rebellion in Morocco against the Umayyads, they established an independent state (CE 744 – 1058) in the area of Tamesna on the Atlantic coast between Safi and Salé under the leadership of…

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: The Midrarid dynasty or Banu Midrar were a Berber dynasty that ruled the Tafilalt region and founded the city of Sijilmasa in 757.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: Up until the 14th century, as the northern terminus for the western trans-Sahara trade route, it was one of the most important trade centres in the Maghreb during the Middle Ages.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: The polity was founded in 710 CE by Salih I ibn Mansur through a Caliphate grant.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: In 859, the kingdom became subject to a 62 ship-strong group of Vikings, who defeated a Moorish force in Nekor that had attempted to interfere with their plunderings in the area.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: His dynasty, the Banū Sālih, thereafter ruled the region until 1019.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: By the second half of the 8th century the westernmost regions of the Maghreb, including present-day Morocco, had been effectively independent of the Umayyad Caliphate since the Khariji-led Berber revolts that started in 739–740.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: The Idrisid dynasty was a Muslim polity centered in Morocco, which ruled from 788 to 974.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: In 789 he founded a settlement south east of Volubilis, called Medinat Fas.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: The western Sanhaja had been converted to Islam some time in the 9th century.

scenes.caption: Photo 1919 · Marrakech
scenes.text: They succeeded in unifying Morocco after it had been divided among several Zenata principalities in the late 10th century, and annexed the Emirate of Sijilmasa and the Barghawata (Tamesna) into their realm.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: Around 1035, the Lamtuna chieftain Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Tifat (alias Tarsina), tried to reunite the Sanhaja desert tribes, but his reign lasted less than three years.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: They laid siege to Marrakesh for forty days until, in April (or May) 1130, the Almoravids sallied from the city and crushed the Almohads in the bloody Battle of al-Buhayra (named after a large garden east of the city).

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: In 1212, the Almohad Caliph Muhammad 'al-Nasir' (1199–1214), the successor of al-Mansur, after an initially successful advance north, was defeated by an alliance of the three Christian kings of Castile, Aragón and Navarre at the…

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: Before his death in 1213, al-Nasir appointed his young ten-year-old son as the next caliph Yusuf II "al-Mustansir".

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: During their stay in the Rif, the Almohad state suffered huge blows, losing large territories to the Christians in Spain, while the Hafsids of Ifriqia broke away in 1229, followed by the Zayyanid dynasty of Tlemcen in 1235.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: In the 13th century, the Kingdom of Castile made several incursions into their territory.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: It was in this period that the Spanish Christians were first able to take the fighting to mainland present-day Morocco: in 1260 and 1267 they attempted an invasion, but both attempts were defeated.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: The Wattasid family had been the autonomous governors of the eastern Rif since the late 13th century, ruling from their base in Tazouta (near present-day Nador).

scenes.caption: Photo 1919 · Marrakech
scenes.text: He went on to found the Kingdom of Fez and establish the dynasty to be succeeded by his son, Mohammed al-Burtuqali, in 1504.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: Mohammad al-Chaykh's son attempted to capture Asilah and Tangier in 1508, 1511 and 1515, but without success.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: From 1509 to 1549, the Saadi rulers had control of only the southern areas.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: While still recognizing the Wattasids as Sultans until 1528, Saadians' growing power led the Wattasids to attack them and, after a decisive battle, to recognize their rule over southern Morocco through the Treaty of Tadla.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: In 1659, Mohammed al-Hajj ibn Abu Bakr al-Dila'i, the head of the zaouia of Dila, was proclaimed sultan of Morocco after the fall of the Saadi dynasty.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: After 1609, approximately 10,000 down-and-out expelled Moriscos arrived from Spain.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: After Janszoon left Salé in 1627, the Moriscos ceased to recognize the authority of the Sultan Zidan al-Nasir, and refused to pay his tithe on their incomes.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925 · Marrakech
scenes.text: After bloody clashes in 1630, an agreement was reached: the election of a Qaid by Andalusians and a new Diwan of 16 members of whom 8 were Andalusians and 8 Hornacheros.

scenes.caption: Photo 1923
scenes.text: In 1844, after the French conquered Algeria, the Franco-Moroccan War took place, with the bombardment of Tangiers, the Battle of Isly, and the bombardment of Mogador.

scenes.caption: Photo 1923
scenes.text: The Hispano-Moroccan War took place from 1859 to 1860, and the subsequent Treaty of Wad Ras led the Moroccan government to take a massive British loan larger than its national reserves to pay off its war debt to Spain.

scenes.caption: Photo 1925
scenes.text: In January 1944, the Istiqlal (Independence) Party, which subsequently provided most of the leadership for the nationalist movement, released a manifesto demanding full independence, national reunification, and a democratic…

scenes.title: What the sources leave out
scenes.text: Before 550 BC, history is not dated in these sources: oral traditions, archaeology and local sources are still to be brought in.
